cells.tense: The care is steady right now, and you're the one holding both sides of it without strain.
cells.ask: offer the tending you give freely to one person who's never been told it mattered.
cells.core:
You're holding two things at once and neither one is losing. Watering one while the other waits its turn, and it's working — not because you've got it under control, but because you actually care about both of them. The ground here is open, nothing planted yet, and you're tending it anyway. That's the whole thing. You're not waiting for something to grow before you start caring for it.

What comes back from tending like this is a kind of permission — you get to let one of these go when it's finished, without it meaning you gave up. The care you've been pouring into both doesn't have to stay split forever. One of them is closer to done than you think. When it's done, letting it rest isn't losing it.
cells.sheetLine: You're caring for both at once, and neither one is losing.

cells.tense: You're already three seasons ahead, bracing for what the ground might do before a single thing is in it.
cells.ask: let one picture of how this turns out go unfinished today, and mean it.
cells.core:
The ground is open and you're treating it like a problem to solve before it becomes one. You've got the harvest planned, the rows drawn, the failures rehearsed — and none of it has happened yet. The care has tipped into managing something that isn't here to manage. You can feel the grip in your hands even when there's nothing in them.

Standing in the same open ground with nothing decided can be a good place to be. You put your hands down, you let it be spring and not harvest, and the space stops feeling like a gap you failed to fill. That version is reachable from here, and it doesn't start with planning harder. It starts with what you've already lived through being enough to dream from. You don't have to invent a future to feel like you're doing this right.
cells.sheetLine: You're managing a future that hasn't arrived yet.

cells.tense: You keep circling back to what you didn't plant, and the ground in front of you looks like someone else's field.
cells.ask: pick one small living thing and tend it badly, just to prove you still can.
cells.core:
The ground is open, and it's been open, and you've stopped kneeling down into it. The kneeling is what you miss and you've been standing at the edge, hands in your pockets, watching other people work their rows. The care didn't go anywhere. It's just not moving through your hands right now, and that's a different thing from having lost it.

An ordinary enough version of this is still available: you put something small in the ground, you show up for it, and one day you notice it grew because you kept coming back. Not a triumph. Just a thing that happened while you were paying attention. That's reachable from where you're standing, and it doesn't ask you to believe in the whole harvest first. Pick one small living thing. Tend it badly. See what happens.
cells.sheetLine: You left the field, but the field didn't leave you.

cells.tense: You're already tending something, hand in the dirt, but you're telling yourself you're just standing nearby.
cells.ask: say out loud that one thing you keep alive is yours, and let someone hear you mean it.
cells.core:
You're doing it right now. The small tending, the keeping something watered, the showing up before you have a name for why — it's all happening through your hands and you talk about it like it arrived on its own. Like you had nothing to do with it. But the ground is being worked, and the one working it is you, and you've never once said so.

The version of this where you know it's yours doesn't look dramatic. You finish something, it feels actually done, and you let that be enough — no audit, no credit check, no waiting for someone to notice. What you tend here is real. Saying so out loud is the only thing missing, and that's a smaller ask than it sounds like.
cells.sheetLine: You're doing the tending, and it's yours.
